## What did the measurement find?

The run covered 25 questions a buyer in AI discovery monitoring and content might ask an AI engine, checked across two engines in September 2026. The headline finding: being named in an AI answer is rare, and being cited as a source is rarer still.

- Of 25 questions, the business was named in 2.
- Of 25 questions, 0 produced a citation of the business's own site.
- Citations of any site appeared on only [4](https://reachkit.app/) of the 25 questions, each one a question that already named a specific rival — comparisons like "AEO Engine vs Meltwater" or "alternatives to AEO Engine."
- The highest number of sites cited on any single question was 3, on the question asking which is better value among three named products.

- Every open, generic question — "which tools should I look at first," "which platforms do people recommend," "on a small budget," "as a team of one," "within a single day of setup" — came back answered but with 0 citations.

The pattern holds across phrasing. Swapping "AI answer visibility platforms" for "search and AI ranking platforms" or "buyer discovery tracking platforms" changed nothing: still answered, still no name, still no citation.

## How was this measured?

The method was simple: ask the same kind of question a real buyer would type, read the answer, and record what it did and didn't contain. Nothing here is a ranking position or a volume count — just what the answer said.

Questions covered five angles: general tool discovery ("what are the best AI discovery monitoring and content tools right now"), budget and team-size framing ("on a small budget," "as a team of one," "without an engineering team"), buyer-fit framing for B[2](https://reachkit.app/)B SaaS and software companies specifically, direct rival comparisons naming AEO Engine and Meltwater, and problem-framed questions ("nothing I have tried helps me understand where AI and search send buyers"). Two engines were queried: ai_mode and chatgpt. The run was taken on a single day, 28 September 2026.

What this does not measure: it does not measure search rank, it does not measure search volume, and it does not score any other company's visibility as a number. It records three things per question — whether the engine answered at all, whether it named this business, and how many sites it cited. It does not track engines beyond those two, and it does not repeat the run across multiple days to show a trend inside this report.

## What does the data look like in full?

The table below groups the 25 questions by type and shows how each group behaved. Every question in a group returned an answer; the columns show whether the business was named and how many sites were cited.

| Question type | Count | Business named | Sites cited |
|---|---|---|---|
| General tool discovery | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| Budget / team-size framing | 8 | 0 | 0 |
| B2B SaaS buyer-fit framing | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| Direct rival comparison | 4 | 0 | up to 3 |
| Problem-framed | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| Business named directly in the question | 2 | 2 | up to 1 |

The two questions that named the business directly were, unsurprisingly, the only ones where it was named back — one asking what the business is and whether it's any good, the other asking if it's a good alternative to a named rival. Even there, a citation only appeared once.

## What does this mean for a buyer?

If you're a buyer asking AI what tool to use in this market, you're far more likely to get an answer with no company named than one with a recommendation. If you're a company selling into this market, that means most of the buyer questions that matter to you are currently producing answers that skip every brand — including the ones already established.

The gap to close isn't a ranking gap. It's a naming gap. Only once a buyer's question already contains a competitor's name does the engine start citing sources — up to 3 of them. That tells you where the opening is: generic, early-stage buyer questions are wide open, because nothing is currently filling them with a citable answer.

For a company with no presence in these answers yet, this is closer to opportunity than to disadvantage. The field is largely uncited. A page that directly answers one of these generic questions, built from your own facts, has somewhere to land.

*Buyer questions, stored with the page (`drafts.meta.faq`):*

**How often do AI answers name any company at all in this market?**

In this run, 4 of 25 questions produced any cited site at all, and those were the ones already naming a rival in the question. The other 21 were answered with no site named.

**Does asking about budget or team size change whether a tool gets named?**

No. Questions framed around a small budget, a team of one, or no engineering team all came back answered with zero citations, same as the general questions.

**Is this the same as a Google ranking?**

No. This measures what an AI engine says in its answer text, not a search results position, and no ranking position is reported here.

**Why would a company want to know this if it isn't named yet?**

Because 21 of 25 questions in this market go unanswered by name, meaning the field is open rather than already won by competitors.

**Does naming a rival in a question change the kind of answer you get?**

Yes. The only questions that produced citations in this run were ones that already named a specific rival, up to 3 sites cited on the highest case.
